The Silurian Period. Running from four hundred and forty-four to four hundred and nineteen million years ago, the Silurian witnessed the colonisation of land by plants for the first time. Humble vascular plants like Cooksonia rooted themselves in barren soil, beginning the transformation of Earth's terrestrial landscape. The period is named after the Silures, an ancient Welsh tribe. Marine life continued to flourish with the rise of jawed fishes, while the first scorpions crept onto land.

Vascular plants with tubes for water transport evolved during the Silurian, marking the first vegetation on land. These were initially small plants, without leaves or roots. Jawed fish, called placoderms, dominated the seas as armored creatures with crude jaw-like structures that became the ancestors of all modern jawed vertebrates. Coral reefs expanded, and the oceans were cooler and more stable than after the Ordovician extinction that preceded this period.

The first arachnids, scorpions, ventured onto land, breathing air and hunting the earliest arthropods. The ozone layer was forming in the upper atmosphere, which made land more habitable by filtering ultraviolet radiation. No large animals colonised land yet; terrestrial life remained confined to small arthropods and primitive plants.

The Silurian follows the Ordovician Period, which ended in mass extinction, and precedes the Devonian Period, the age of fishes and the further conquest of land by animals.
